headline: Reflecting Pool case closed. For good.
summary: A Washington judge dismissed the vandalism case against David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, with prejudice on Thursday, so no one can refile it. The Justice Department had dropped it after finding contractors botched the pool's resealing. Trump called that "a disgrace" and pressed to revive it. Judge Todd Edelman cited that pressure.
cover_answer: He tried. The judge closed the case so no one can.
table_question: A boss orders you to punish someone you think did nothing. Then what?

5-7.script: A man in Washington says he rode his bike past a long, flat pool and touched a strip of lining that was peeling off. The people in charge said he wrecked the pool and took him to court. Then they found out the workers had rushed the job, and on Thursday a judge said the case is over, for good. The grown-ups sorted it out.
5-7.why: One peeling strip and one judge. The ending is fair.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a picture: a long flat pool and a strip peeling off it. Piaget's stage cannot yet weigh a president against a judge, so the script does not try: the workers rushed the job and the man did nothing wrong. Expect "did he get in trouble?" For a while. Not now.

8-12.script: In June the Reflecting Pool's new lining peeled. Prosecutors charged David Hearn, who says he only touched a loose strip. Then inspectors blamed the contractor's rushed job, and the case was dropped. Trump pushed to recharge Hearn, so a judge closed it for good, like a referee's final call.
8-12.why: Peel, charge, drop, push, final whistle.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether rules apply to the people on top, and this chain asks it: the pool peeled, charges, the inspectors blamed the contractor, the president pushed to bring the case back. The final whistle is the mechanism: with prejudice means no refiling. Expect "why only him?" The judge said it: he gave to Democrats.

13-17.script: Can the president make prosecutors charge someone? He tried: his own US attorney dropped the Reflecting Pool case, and Trump called that "stupid" and named David Hearn's gifts to Democrats. A judge closed it for good, citing that pressure. Second: should a judge put that in writing?
13-17.why: Prosecutor, president, judge: who answers to whom.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the president picks the prosecutors, and the prosecutors are supposed to answer to the evidence, and the script sits in that gap. Argument is practised, Kuhn's point, so the second question hands them the judge's own words. Expect "so was it vandalism?" The inspectors blamed the contractor.

5-7.a: The people who checked say no. The workers who fixed it rushed the job, and the lining peeled.

8-12.a: No. With prejudice means no refiling. The judge chose that.

8-12.q: Why did Trump want him charged?
8-12.a: He said vandals did it, and that Hearn gives money to Democrats.

13-17.a: He tried, in public. The judge closed the case for good.
Three others, also dropped. Hearn had faced up to 10 years.
